overview: A one-page Department of State list of papers filed under 894.7962 concerning Japanese aviation infrastructure and military air facilities from 1932 to 1936. The indexed papers cover repeated proposals and developments for a commercial airport at Nagoya, reports on aerodromes or landing fields at Nankai, Kamitsu, and Ehime, Japanese naval plans for five additional air bases facing the perceived Soviet air threat over the Sea of Japan, and an incident involving Assistant Naval Attaché Ralph Andrew Ofstie near the Kure air station. Several entries are notes directing researchers to related decimal-file numbers rather than substantive documents contained in this bundle.

subfiles.title: List of papers concerning aviation landing fields in Japan
subfiles.about: An internal index lists nine reports and cross-references concerning commercial airports, landing fields, aerodromes, and military air bases in Japan between 1932 and 1936.
subfiles.summary: The sheet indexes reports from Nagoya, Tianjin, Japan, and Kobe concerning proposed or developing aviation facilities. Three entries concern the projected commercial airport at Nagoya, while others address an aerodrome at Nankai, a landing field at Kamitsu in Hyogo Prefecture, and a new Ehime aerodrome. It also records the Japanese Navy's decision to add five air bases in response to Soviet air power and cross-references a memorandum about charges that Assistant Naval Attaché Ralph Andrew Ofstie photographed the Kure air station from a train traveling between Shimonoseki and Tokyo.

interest: This sheet is useful as a compact finding aid to State Department reporting on the expansion of Japanese civil and military aviation infrastructure during the 1930s. It shows how ostensibly local airport developments were catalogued alongside strategic concerns about Soviet air power and counterintelligence sensitivities surrounding military installations. The Ofstie entry is especially notable because it connects aviation facilities with surveillance allegations and directs researchers to a separate personnel-related file; the other cross-references likewise reveal relationships among otherwise dispersed decimal-file records.
